voices.speaker: Gen. John Bell Hood
voices.quote: I hereupon decided … to make that same afternoon another and final effort to overtake and rout him, and drive him in the Big Harpeth river at Franklin.
voices.context: Writing years later of the decision he took on the Columbia Pike after Schofield slipped past him in the night at Spring Hill.

voices.speaker: Maj. Gen. Benjamin F. Cheatham
voices.quote: I could easily see all the movements of the Federals and readily trace their line. I saw that they were well fortified and in a strong position. I felt that we would take a desperate chance if we attempted to dislodge them.
voices.context: Reading the Federal works from the crest of Winstead Hill, two miles out.

voices.speaker: Maj. Gen. Nathan Bedford Forrest
voices.quote: General Hood, if you give me one strong division of infantry with my cavalry, I will agree to flank the Federals from their works within two hours' time.
voices.context: Arguing against a frontal assault. Hood refused him.

voices.speaker: Maj. Gen. Patrick R. Cleburne
voices.quote: General, I will take the works or fall in the attempt.
voices.context: To Hood, having first called the assault a terrible and useless waste of life.

voices.speaker: Maj. Gen. Patrick R. Cleburne
voices.role: Replying to Brig. Gen. Daniel C. Govan
voices.quote: Well, Govan, if we are to die, let us die like men.
voices.context: Govan had just said: “Well, General, few of us will ever return to Arkansas to tell the story of this battle.” Within the hour Cleburne was dead on the ground in front of the cotton gin.

voices.speaker: Capt. John K. Shellenberger
voices.role: Company B, 64th Ohio — Conrad's brigade, in the advanced line
voices.quote: We plainly saw the movements of a large part of Stewart's corps. They first came into view from behind a body of timber over towards the river, deploying from column on the right by file into line on double quick.
voices.context: Watching the Army of Tennessee form for the attack from the exposed forward position half a mile in front of the main works.

voices.speaker: Pvt. John M. Copley
voices.role: Company B, 49th Tennessee — Quarles' Brigade, Walthall's Division
voices.quote: A profound silence pervaded the entire army; it was simply awful, reminding one of those sickening lulls which precede a tremendous thunderstorm.
voices.context: In the ranks in the minutes before the advance stepped off.

voices.speaker: Col. James D. Porter
voices.quote: It was the grandest sight I ever saw when our army marched over the hill and reached the open field base. Each division unfolded itself into a single line of battle with as much steadiness as if forming for dress parade.
voices.context: Eighteen brigades — some twenty thousand men — stepping off across two miles of open ground with the bands playing and the colors up.

voices.speaker: 36th Illinois Volunteers
voices.role: Regimental history, behind the main works
voices.quote: a tornado heralded by clouds of darkness and muttering thunders
voices.context: How the advance sounded to the men waiting behind the parapet as it filled the plain to the south.

voices.speaker: Capt. John K. Shellenberger
voices.quote: It ran along the line so rapidly that it reminded me of a train of powder burning. I instantly sprang to my feet and looked to the front. They were coming on the run, emitting the shrill rebel charging yell.
voices.context: Wagner's two forward brigades break and run for the works — with the Confederates coming in behind them, so close that the main line could not fire.

voices.speaker: Capt. John K. Shellenberger
voices.quote: I fell headlong into the ditch just as our line there opened fire. The roar of their guns was sweeter than music and I chuckled with satisfaction as I thought, “Now, Rebs, your turn has come.”
voices.context: Reaching the safety of the main works one step ahead of the assault.

voices.speaker: Col. John S. Casement
voices.quote: stand here like rocks, and whip the h—— out of them
voices.context: Holding his brigade at the parapet east of the pike, where the repeating rifles of his line cut down the attack as fast as it came on.
voices.place: The Federal left of the pike

voices.speaker: Maj. Gen. William W. Loring
voices.quote: Great God! Do I command cowards?
voices.context: Sitting his horse in front of the works on the Confederate right, where his division had been shot to pieces against the railroad cut and the osage-orange hedge.
voices.place: The Federal right of the pike

voices.speaker: Pvt. Sam R. Watkins
voices.quote: Kind reader, right here my pen, and courage, and ability fail me. I shrink from butchery.
voices.context: Watkins wrote a whole memoir of the war and could not bring himself to describe this hour of it.

voices.speaker: Pvt. Sam R. Watkins
voices.quote: The twilight of evening had begun to gather as a precursor of the coming blackness of midnight darkness that was to envelop a scene so sickening and horrible …
voices.context: The sun had set at 4:33. The moon was two days past new. Most of what followed was fought blind.

voices.speaker: Capt. John K. Shellenberger
voices.quote: The front rank did nothing but fire. The empty guns were passed back to those in rear who reloaded them. The rear rank was kneeling with guns at a ready.
voices.context: Four and five ranks deep behind the parapet, the Federals worked a relay of loaded rifles into the dark for hours.

voices.speaker: Pvt. B. F. Thompson
voices.quote: Never before did a command of the approximate strength of Casement's in as short a period of time kill and wound as many.
voices.context: Written of the ground in front of his own brigade.
voices.place: The Federal left of the pike

voices.speaker: Pvt. Sam R. Watkins
voices.quote: Dead soldiers filled the entrenchments. The firing was kept up until after midnight, and gradually died out.
voices.context: The attack was spent hours before the shooting stopped. Schofield's army crossed the Harpeth in the dark and was gone by dawn.

epilogueVoices.speaker: Capt. John K. Shellenberger
epilogueVoices.quote: The ground near the ditch was so thickly covered with bodies that I had to pick my steps carefully to avoid treading on some of them. The air was filled with the moans of the wounded.

epilogueVoices.speaker: Pvt. Sam R. Watkins
epilogueVoices.quote: when the morrow's sun began to light up the eastern sky with its rosy hues, and we looked over the battlefield, O, my God! what did we see! It was a grand holocaust of death.
